When the default memberwise copying of data is allowed for an object that contains pointers, it can lead to a shallow copying of the data. This means that the copied object will point to the same memory location as the original object, rather than having its own separate copy of the data.

As we discussed earlier, this can cause problems if the original object is modified or deleted, because the copied object will also be affected. To avoid this issue, it's often necessary to implement a deep copy, where a separate copy of the data is made for the new object.

In the context of the IntCell class, if the default memberwise copying of data is allowed, it could lead to a shallow copying of the data. However, as we saw in the course materials, the IntCell class can accept the defaults because it doesn't contain any pointers. But if a class contains pointers, it's generally necessary to implement a deep copy to avoid the problems associated with shallow copying. Does this clarify things for you?

It seems like you're asking about the difference between value parameters and constant reference parameters. 

In C++, when you pass an argument to a function, you can pass it by value or by reference. When you pass by value, a copy of the original argument is made and passed to the function. This is what's meant by "value parameters." 

On the other hand, when you pass by constant reference, a reference to the original argument is passed to the function, but the function is not allowed to modify the original argument. This is what's meant by "constant reference parameters." 

Constant reference parameters are useful when you want to avoid making a copy of the argument, which can be expensive for large objects. They're also useful when you want to ensure that the function doesn't modify the original argument. 

In contrast, value parameters are useful when you want the function to have its own copy of the argument, which it can modify without affecting the original argument. 

So, to summarize: value parameters involve making a copy of the argument, while constant reference parameters involve passing a reference to the original argument without allowing it to be modified. Does this clarify things for you?
